body.content: Last summer, I walked past a SET store with an advertisement:
The brand everyone was wearing in your pilates class this morning.

The ad unfurled a longer thought. Everyone's consumption habits appear the same these days. People are converging in the music they listen to, the hobbies they pursue, the vacations they chase + {...} = the same perfectly fungible lives.

When the best thing from any one place can reach anywhere, the same things end up everywhere. McDonald's was a Southern Californian drive-in. The Hass avocado was a single tree in a Pasadena backyard. The Eames chair was made in a Pacific Palisades studio. Global products have replaced local texture.

You see it on any college campus. At USC, students wear the same brands (Aviator Nation, Golden Goose, Madhappy), eat at the same restaurants (Sugarfish and Élephante), and are transfixed by the same shows (Love Island). New grads move to NYC for work and live in the same studio apartments with white walls and exposed brick.

What's lost in all this is emergence. Meaningful life experiences and exceptional creative work are both emergent phenomena. Both come from the same asymmetry: unconstrained imagination and disciplined execution. Pre-fill the imagination, and the output becomes nothing more than a permutation.
Life is defined by ambiguity and agency, and traipsing through a world optimized for efficiency lacks both. The goal is to resist fungibility.
